Oil rises amid growing tensions between Saudis and Iran-backed Houthis
A Saudi-led coalition reportedly struck Houthi energy terminals and fuel reserves in Yemen.
U.S. Central Command rejected Iran's claims that the Strait of Hormuz is under Tehran's control and that any approaching U.S. Navy warships would be "sunk."
Oil may rally another $20-$25 due to the Iran conflict, hedge fund manager and notable commodity trader Paul Tudor Jones said on on CNBC's "Squawk Box."
Iran's medium-sized oil tankers continue to wait off the coast of Bandar Abbas at the Strait of Hormuz in Hormozgan Province, Iran on September 09, 2026.
Oil prices were higher on Wednesday morning, pulling back from earlier gains, as investors digested the International Energy Agency's latest monthly report on the shape of the oil market.
Brent crude futures , the international benchmark, were 20 cents higher at $105.89 a barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate was up $1.27 to $95.41 a barrel.
The IEA's October Oil Market Report, published Wednesday, warned that constraints on diesel markets could continue well into 2027, with fresh attacks on Saudi Arabia threatening to derail a recovery on the supply side of the global oil market.
Fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-backed Houthis continues to escalate, with the Saudi Ministry of Energy saying Wednesday that an administrative building belonging to oil giant Saudi Aramco had been attacked overnight. No injuries were reported at the site in Dhahran, a city on Saudi Arabia's eastern coast.
It follows a series of Houthi attacks on the Saudi capital Riyadh over the past week, including a fatal strike on the city's international airport.
According to Al Jazeera, Houthi energy terminals and fuel reserves in Yemen were struck by a Saudi-led coalition, though a spokesperson said that precautions were taken to avoid "collateral damage on civilians."
Tensions also continued to simmer between the U.S. and Iran.
U.S. Central Command rejected claims by the commander of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy that the Strait of Hormuz is under Iran's control and that any approaching U.S. Navy warships would be "sunk."
"RGC's navy commander has no navy," CENTCOM said in an X post , adding that "American forces and regional partners clearly control the Strait of Hormuz."
Oil may rally another $20-$25 due to the Iran conflict, hedge fund manager and noted commodity trader Paul Tudor Jones said on CNBC's "Squawk Box."
"I am long oil... bullish oil...I think it can rally another $20 or $25 bucks," said the founder and chief investment officer of Tudor Investment.
"If something to ameliorate the situation was going to happen, it would have happened already before the midterms," he added.

items.title: Starlink restrictions in Ukraine war linked to political situation, Zelensky aide says
items.summary: Elon Musk's system allows Kyiv to protect Ukrainian skies and effectively guide drones to Russian targets.
items.content:
Figure caption, Watch: What we know about Russia's overnight strikes on Ukraine
By Jaroslav Lukiv Â  and Â  Dan Johnson ,Â  Ukraine correspondent in Kyiv
New restrictions on the speed at which some of Ukraine's weapons can travel and still connect to the Starlink internet network have disrupted Ukraine's battlefield "missions", President Volodymyr Zelensky's adviser has warned.
Serhiy Beskrestnov said Ukraine had not been told about speed limits set overnight at 100mph (160km/h) by Elon Musk's SpaceX company.
Starlink is a vital tool allowing Kyiv to effectively guide drones to Russian targets and also protect Ukrainian skies.
Beskrestnov said SpaceX's move "cannot be a coincidence and is related to the current political situation". The firm has not commented.
In Wednesday's post on Telegram, Beskrestnov said SpaceX had "implemented overnight a speed limit on Starlink terminals" and this had already resulted in "the disruption of a number of missions".
This comes as at least 600,000 people across Ukraine were left without electricity after deadly overnight Russian missile and drone strikes, Zelensky said.
He said "critical" energy infrastructure had been hit in Kyiv and the capital region, and in the north-eastern city of Kharkiv â despite US President Donald Trump's claim on Sunday that an "energy ceasefire" was in place between Russia and Ukraine.
Three people were killed in Kyiv, local officials said. Russia said its "massive" strikes had hit communications and energy facilities used by Ukraine's military.
Later on Wednesday, at least six people were killed in a Russian drone strike on a warehouse in the north-western city of Lutsk, local officials said.
Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.
In the follow-up post, Zelensky's adviser stressed that Starlink was the most effective tool for enabling interceptors to shoot down Russia's newly developed jet-propelled drones.
Image caption, The Starlink system has become a vital tool to give troops in Ukraine internet access
A source in the Ukrainian defence ministry later told the BBC: "Last night, we detected restrictions affecting Starlink connectivity at speeds above 160 km/h." The source added that the "root cause" of the issue was being investigated.
Defence ministry sources later explained that "once a vehicle or asset exceeds this [160km/h] threshold speed, the terminal loses its connection".
They told the BBC that this made it more difficult to carry out drone operations, "specifically interceptors and middle-strike drones", and also degraded "capabilities for front line logistics, reconnaissance, and signal relaying".
In February, Musk's decision to deny Russian forces access to Starlink blunted Moscow's advance in Ukraine and caused confusion among Russian commanders.
Musk's SpaceX has not commented on the reported speed restrictions.
Zelensky has said the US threatened to restrict intelligence sharing if he did not sign up to Trump's energy ceasefire. Trump on Tuesday denied that Washington was withholding intelligence.
Overnight, Russia had launched 39 ballistic and cruise missiles and 128 drones, and that four of those missiles and 115 drones had been shot down, according to Ukraine's air force.
It is the second night in a row Kyiv has been hit by Russian missiles, and came as Zelensky prepared to meet UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham at Downing Street on Wednesday to discuss accelerating air defence supplies to Kyiv.
During the past two nights, ballistic missiles have struck targets in the Ukrainian capital without any warning, before air raid sirens could be sounded.
Ukraine relies on US satellite systems to track Russian missiles in order to issue alerts and to try to shoot them down.
Image caption, People watched the emergency services at work at the scene of the strikes in Ukraine
Meanwhile, the Russian defence ministry said 902 Ukrainian drones had been shot down overnight over a number of Russian regions, including the capital Moscow and Crimea â Ukraine's southern peninsula annexed by Russia in 2014.
On Sunday, Trump wrote in a post on social media: "Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!"
Zelensky has since repeatedly said Ukraine is ready to halt its strikes on Russian oil refineries and other energy facilities if Moscow did the same.
But Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has said Ukraine does not deserve the "respite" a ceasefire would bring. Under any truce, he added, Europe would be able to "pump [Ukraine] with new weapons", enabling it to continue the war.

Ukraine raises alarm over Starlink limits disrupting military operations
For the second time this week, Ukraine didn't receive advance warning from partners of Russian ballistic missile attacks, President Zelenskyy said.
Zelenskyy's defense tech advisor Serhii Beskrestnov suggested limits on SpaceX's Starlink were to blame for the lack of advance warning.
Meanwhile, hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians are without power as of Wednesday morning after Russian attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure overnight, despite Trump's "energy ceasefire."
Ukraine has accused Elon Musk's SpaceX of imposing new restrictions on its Starlink satellite internet service without warning, disrupting Ukrainian military operations.
It comes as Russia intensifies attacks on the country's energy infrastructure despite President Donald Trump's proposed "energy ceasefire."
Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on defense technology, said Wednesday that SpaceX has implemented a speed limit on Starlink terminals in motion without notifying Ukrainian defense forces, disrupting some missions.
Meanwhile, Russia unleashed an attack on Ukrainian energy infrastructure overnight, leaving at least 600,000 people without power in the Kyiv and Kharkiv regions, raising further questions about the "energy ceasefire" announced by Trump on Sunday.
"There is significant damage to facilities and equipment – at 26 facilities of our power system and four facilities in the oil and gas sector," Zelenskyy said in a post on X early Wednesday.
He highlighted a targeted ballistic missile strike against the energy infrastructure that Zelenskyy said should have been covered by the "energy ceasefire" announced by President Donald Trump on Sunday.
"The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale – Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States," Zelenskyy said.
The attack comes after the Ukrainian president on Monday accused Russia of violating Trump's proposal that the adversaries stop attacking each other's energy facilities to help bring down the cost of oil and diesel.
Both Russian and Ukrainian authorities initially denied any knowledge of an energy ceasefire agreement. Ukraine has since welcomed such a deal, while Russian authorities said talks are ongoing, without confirming whether they have reached an agreement.
Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Monday: "Regarding the status of this agreement, we can refer to Zelensky's reaction. When asked the same question, he said he had not heard of such an agreement, would welcome clarification and was ready for a ceasefire," according to the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
Zelenskyy also said that for the second time this week, Ukraine received no advance warning about Russian ballistic missile launches. The latest unflagged strike on Kyiv damaged a residential building and killed one person and injured six, Zelenskyy said.
Ukraine's Beskrestnov said that the Starlink speed restriction currently applies to the StarShield military service package and is set at 100 mph, or about 160 km/h.
"It is clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is related to the current political situation," Beskrestnov said on Telegram. "SpaceX is likely to have taken such measures at the request of the Trump administration," he added in a separate post.
SpaceX and the White House have been contacted for comment.

items.title: U.S. may have withheld warnings to Ukraine of Russian strikes that killed 6, cut power to 600,000, sources say - CBS News
items.summary: U.S. may have withheld warnings to Ukraine of Russian strikes that killed 6, cut power to 600,000, sources say  CBS News
items.content:
The U.S. may have intentionally withheld early warnings this week of Russian strikes on Ukraine , multiple sources familiar with the matter told CBS News.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine "received no advance warning from our partners" when Russia launched a ballistic missile barrage at Kyiv and other locations early Tuesday.
The sources said American officials told their Ukrainian counterparts the system used to detect Russian missile launches had failed due to "bad weather." Ukrainian officials, speaking on the condition of anonymity given the sensitivity of the topic, told CBS News they did not believe the excuse, and they accused the U.S. instead of "playing" with the system.
When Russia launched another wave of ballistic missiles around 3 a.m. local time on Wednesday, the sources said the U.S. early warning system appeared to be working again.
Ukrainian rescuers and paramedics carry a wounded resident at the site of a Russian missile strike on an apartment building in Kyiv, Oct. 14, 2026, amid the Russian invasion of Ukraine.
The sources said the U.S. had failed to provide intelligence on Russian ballistic missile launches during one previous instance earlier this year, citing the need to focus more resources on the Middle East.
Zelenskyy said Wednesday that Russia launched more than 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 attack drones and loitering munitions during the overnight attack, primarily targeting energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv and Kharkiv, killing six people and leaving some 600,000 without power.
President Trump, asked Tuesday if the U.S. had stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine, said: "No, we haven't. We help them, but we're really helping them get to a final answer. We want the war ended."
"We are helping them, and we are sharing intel. We want the war to end, so we're working with them and with Russia on getting the war to end," Mr. Trump said.
Russia started launching strikes soon after Mr. Trump said in a social media post on Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an "energy ceasefire."
Ukrainian firefighters extinguish a blaze at the site of a Russian missile strike on an apartment building in Kyiv, Oct. 14, 2026, amid the Russian invasion of Ukraine.
Earlier this week, the Trump administration threatened to stop sharing intelligence and to halt the purchase of U.S.-made weapons by European allies for Ukraine via the PURL procurement system if Ukraine did not stop deep strikes against Russian energy infrastructure, a European and a Ukrainian official told CBS News.
Ukraine relies on U.S. intelligence for both offensive and defensive military capabilities, including data from satellites and aircraft sensors used to identify launches of Russian aircraft and missiles. Sources familiar with the matter told CBS News the U.S. had not ceased intelligence sharing with Ukraine overall — calling the lack of a warning about this week's attacks a specific incident.
Ukrainian officials and soldiers also told CBS News that Ukraine's military had started experiencing difficulties Tuesday night and Wednesday morning with Starlink, the satellite technology owned by SpaceX's Elon Musk.
In an interview with CBS News earlier this year, Ukraine's former minister of defense Mykhailo Fedorov said Starlink was one of Ukraine's most important technologies, as it allows Ukrainian soldiers to communicate and carry out strikes in environments saturated by electronic warfare.
"On the night of 14 October, without warning the Defence Forces, SpaceX unilaterally restricted the operation of Starshield terminals ('military package') while in motion. This complicates UAV missions, particularly interceptors and middle-strike drones, and reduces capabilities for frontline logistics, reconnaissance and signal relay," sources in Ukraine's Ministry of Defense told CBS News. "At present, the Ministry of Defence is in contact with the United States, SpaceX and NATO partners, is collecting data from all units, and backup communication channels are being tested and put into use."
The Starlink restrictions were first reported by the Kyiv Independent and the Financial Times. CBS News has reached out to SpaceX, the White House, and the Pentagon for comment.
On Wednesday, as President Zelenskyy arrived in the United Kingdom to meet with Prime Minister Andy Burnham and other officials, he called for a U.S. response to the recent Russian strikes.
"The strike was absolutely deliberate and indicative in its scale — such a demonstrative disrespect from Russia toward America has never happened before. Russia does not consider the statements of the President of America to be strong," he wrote on X. "We ask America and EVERYONE in the world who does not close their eyes to reality to respond, and to respond harshly."
This story published first on CBS News at 8:58 a.m. on Oct. 14, 2026.

items.content:
A production line at the Mercedes-Benz factory in Rastatt, Germany. Photograph: Christoph Steitz/Reuters
A production line at the Mercedes-Benz factory in Rastatt, Germany. Photograph: Christoph Steitz/Reuters
Excluding UK from ‘Made in Europe’ law will hurt entire EU car industry, Mercedes boss warns
Ola Källenius says it will ‘weaken the industry on both sides’ ahead of act intended to counter non-EU competition
Locking the UK out of the EU’s flagship industrial “Made in Europe” legislation would amount to a “deliberate choice” by EU leaders to “hurt” the car industry across the bloc, the head of Mercedes-Benz has said.
Speaking in his capacity as president of the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA), Ola Källenius said such a move would “weaken the industry on both sides”.
He was speaking just weeks before political leaders hope to reach agreement on the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), potentially keeping the UK car industry out of key contracts in the EU.
The act, known as the Made in Europe law, aims to protect local industry by countering competition from outside the EU.
It is mainly aimed at China , which is now enjoying a £1bn a day trade surplus with the EU, but could cause problems for the EU’s close allies including the UK, Norway, Turkey and Switzerland.
“It does not make any sense … We would hurt our industry in the UK and the EU. That would be a deliberate choice to worsen the competitiveness of your own [EU] industry,” Källenius said at an annual briefing in Brussels on the state of the car industry.
“We are talking about how we industrialise more in Europe, how we build local supply chains, that is what the IAA is all about,” he added.
Andy Burnham has been lobbying hard to get the UK included in the Made in Europe legislation but is hitting resistance, particularly from France.
The prime minister intends to raise it at the UK-EU summit on 20 November and is hoping it is not too late, even though EU leaders are aiming for political agreement on the current text by December.
Last month, the EU urged the UK to follow the bloc and impose tariffs on imported Chinese vehicles, which it introduced in 2024. It argued this would help the UK’s case to be included in Made in Europe as it would align more closely with the EU on key trading sectors.
But the UK business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said on a trip to India that this was not on the cards at the moment.
‘Made in Europe’ law threatens UK plans for reset with EU
The ACEA is also lobbying for an urgent suspension of plans to introduce 10% tariffs on UK electric vehicles (EVs) imported to the EU, and EU EVs exported to the UK.
“We are getting very anxious about it. The deadline is in less than three months’ time. We have our feet to the fire in terms of the tariffs. All our manufacturers are worried,” said Jonathan O’Riordan, the ACEA’s international trade director.
The tariff schedule is written into the post-Brexit Trade and Cooperation Agreement (TCA) as a way of incentivising the industry on both sides of the Channel to speed up the production of batteries, which can represent about 45% of the cost of a new car.
Under the TCA, car exports on both sides are tariff-free if they are mainly made in Europe, but with the EU and the UK unable to produce sufficient electric batteries to compete with China, cars exported to each other’s market would be subject to a 10% tariff from next year.
The tariff was originally due to come into force in 2024 but was suspended for three years to give the car industry more time.
The car industry says it needs a further two- or three-year suspension urgently.
Meanwhile, concern has intensified in the EU in the last three months over China’s trade surplus with the bloc, with a threat of trade barriers leading to an agreement on Friday between Beijing and Brussels to reduce sales of hybrid electric cars by half over four years.
One official said the time to rebalance trade by increasing EU exports was gone. “No amount of champagne [exports] is going to revitalise the relationship [with China],” a senior EU official told a separate trade policy briefing in Brussels.

items.title: Russia arrests Japanese journalist on spying charges
items.summary: The Hokkaido Shimbun journalist is accused of collecting information on Moscow's defence capabilities for Tokyo.
items.content:
Image caption, The journalist, identified as Yuki Imai from the Hokkaido Shimbun, was detained in the far eastern region of Sakhalin
Russian authorities have arrested a Japanese journalist on suspicion of espionage, accusing him of gathering information related to Moscow's defence capabilities for Tokyo.
The journalist, identified as Yuki Imai from the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper, was detained in the far-eastern Sakhalin region, a day before he was due to leave Russia. He was flown to Moscow where a court ordered he be placed in pre-trial detention, Russian reports say.
Japan says it is still seeking details about the arrest, and has not been able to contact Imai.
The arrest comes as tensions worsen between the two nations after Russian leader Vladimir Putin visited the disputed Kuril Islands , claimed by both countries, in August.
Russian authorities allege that Imai "acted on the instructions of [Japan's] national intelligence service" to gather information about people involved in a special military operation on the Kuril Islands, state news agency TASS reported.
The Kuril islands sit between Hokkaido in northern Japan and Russia's Kamchatka Peninsula. The archipelago is administered by Russia, but four of the southernmost islands are claimed by Japan, which calls them the Northern Territories.
Russia's FSB security agency published footage showing three masked men in black uniforms storming a hotel room and handcuffing a man. The video then shows him being accompanied onto a plane before appearing in a cage in a Moscow court. It did not say when he was detained or when the court hearing took place.
Imai will be remanded until 12 December, before his trial begins, according to Interfax, another Russian news agency.
Those convicted of espionage in Russia can be sentenced to up to 20 years in prison.
"Tokyo's attempts to use its correspondents in Russia, who hold foreign journalist status, to gather information aimed at undermining our country's security are regrettable," Russian foreign ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said in a statement on Tuesday.
"We cannot help but point out that today's incident is not an isolated one," she noted, but did not name other journalists or media outlets that are allegedly involved in similar activity.
Japan has not commented at length on the arrest. Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara told a press briefing that Japan did not know about the arrest until the announcement and had had no contact yet with the journalist.
Imai's published work has covered Russia's relations with North Korea and life in Sakhalin.
Hokkaido Shimbun ran a report on the arrest without naming the reporter. "We are still confirming the details. Ensuring the reporter's safety is our top priority," it said in response to the BBC's queries.
Russia and Japan have been locked in a dispute over the Kurils for decades, and it is the main reason Moscow and Tokyo did not sign a peace treaty after World War Two.
Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi sharply criticised Putin's visit â his first-ever to the islands â saying it "wounded the feelings of the Japanese people" and is "incompatible with Japan's consistent position on the Northern Territories".
Moscow dismissed her remarks as "politically inappropriate" and "legally unfounded".
Over the years, attempts to resolve the territorial dispute have made little progress. Bilateral ties have also remained frosty, with Japan imposing sanctions against Russia for its invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Last week, Moscow again angered Tokyo by requesting the extradition of the president of the International Criminal Court (ICC), who is Japanese.
The president Tomoko Akane, along with other ICC officials, has been placed on Russia's wanted list since 2023 after the court issued an arrest warrant for Putin over war crimes in Ukraine.
In 2023, Russia detained The Wall Street Journal's Evan Gershkovich on espionage charges and later sentenced him to 16 years in prison.
Gershkovich, a US citizen, was released in a 2024 prisoner swap, the largest exchange since the Cold War ended in 1991.
In 2019, Moscow detained an unnamed Japanese journalist from Kyodo News on suspicion of attempting to obtain military secrets. The journalist, who was picked up in Vladivostok, was ordered to leave the country within 72 hours.

items.title: The Iran war's unexpected impact on US defenses against China threat downplayed by top Army leader - Fox News
items.summary: <a href="https://news.google.
items.content:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.
Amid growing concerns that the Iran war is drawing away critical U.S. defenses from China's doorstep, the Army's top commander in the Pacific says the forces are using this unexpected opportunity to modernize.
Gen. Ronald Clark, commander of U.S. Army Pacific, provided his assessment that diverting Patriot missile defenses to the Iran war has not increased risk to forces in the Indo-Pacific despite concerns about deployments impacting America's readiness for potential conflict with China.
"Actually, it's given us an opportunity to modernize our systems here," Clark told Fox News Digital during a small-group interview at the Association of the United States Army's annual conference in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday.
Patriot systems have been redeployed from the Indo-Pacific to support operations in the Middle East, while U.S. forces in South Korea have also sent Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) interceptors to the region.
U.S. Army Gen. Ronald Clark, commanding general of U.S. Army Pacific, speaks with NSS guests during National Security Seminar Week at the U.S. Army War College in Carlisle, Pa., June 4, 2026. (Elizabeth Bukowski/US Army War College)
An October Congressional Research Service report cited estimates that U.S. forces had expended roughly 1,700 Patriot and 200 THAAD interceptors during the conflict, while the Congressional Budget Office estimated that the military had used between half and two-thirds of certain interceptor inventories. The Pentagon's inspector general has cited strategic inventory shortfalls and manufacturing bottlenecks stemming from the conflict, raising questions about how quickly the U.S. could replenish its defenses in the event of another major confrontation.
Clark said the deployments are giving Patriot crews firsthand experience defending against enemy attacks, while equipment upgrades are expanding what individual batteries can accomplish.
He said an upgraded Patriot battery can now provide coverage that previously required an entire battalion, though he did not specify whether he was referring to geographic coverage or the number of threats the system can engage.
Asked whether recent diplomatic progress between President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping had changed his assessment of the threat from China, Clark said he believes the People's Liberation Army (PLA) is continuing its build-up.
"Well, I believe they're continuing to prepare," Clark said.
XI PREPARES CHINA ‘FOR BATTLE’ AS EXPERT WARNS OF GRAVE DANGER FACING US AHEAD OF DC SUMMIT
U.S. President Donald Trump greets Chinese President Xi Jinping ahead of a bilateral meeting at Gimhae Air Base on October 30, 2025, in Busan, South Korea. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
The assessment comes weeks after Trump welcomed Xi to Washington for a high-profile state visit that produced new trade agreements and commitments to improve military communications. But the diplomatic progress has not resolved tensions over Taiwan and China's growing military reach across the Indo-Pacific, where American commanders continue preparing for a potential conflict.
Clark did not say whether China's military preparations had accelerated or whether diplomatic outreach had changed Beijing's intentions. He emphasized that the U.S. military's responsibility is to remain ready for a potential conflict while working to prevent one.
TAIWAN ANALYSTS SAY TRUMP-XI SUMMIT PRODUCED NO POLICY SHIFT BUT REAL TEST LIES AHEAD
"Hopefully my legacy in this job is that when we walk away from command of USARPAC, that the deterrent posture of our command is such that we have not just prevented war, but we're preventing war in the future," Clark said.
Clark said Adm. Samuel Paparo, commander of U.S. Indo-Pacific Command, recently discussed reviving disaster-management exchanges between the U.S. Army and China's PLA during talks with his Chinese counterpart.
The exchanges would provide an opportunity for American and Chinese military personnel to work together on disaster response, restoring a channel of direct engagement that Clark said he hoped to see revived.
"If you're able to have a conversation with your adversaries, you're able to share information with them in a way that makes them not want to fight," Clark said.
A Philippine Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources vessel, labeled DA-BFAR MMOV 3015, navigates in proximity to another ship during a maritime encounter. (Chinese Coast Guard)
He said U.S. Army Pacific would be responsible for coordinating the exchanges with its Chinese counterparts if the effort moves forward. He did not announce a date or say that Beijing had formally agreed to resume the program.
The U.S. and Chinese militaries have periodically conducted disaster-management exchanges in the past, including an event hosted by the Army at Joint Base Lewis-McChord in Washington state in 2017.
"The cost of going to war is just so high that it's our duty to, one, be absolutely prepared for that eventuality, but two, to prevent that from happening," Clark said.
The diplomatic outreach comes amid continued confrontations between Chinese and Philippine forces in the South China Sea. As Fox News Digital previously reported, the Philippines tracked 101 Chinese navy and coast guard vessels around disputed waters in September, nearly double the number recorded in August. More recently, Philippine authorities accused Chinese forces of obstructing maritime operations and carrying out dangerous maneuvers near Philippine aircraft.
CHINESE MILITARY ACTIVITY NEARLY DOUBLES AROUND KEY US ALLY IN DISPUTED WATERS
Meanwhile, the Army has been expanding its capabilities across the Indo-Pacific, positioning additional forces and equipment closer to potential flashpoints as part of its effort to deter Chinese aggression.
China launched rockets near Taiwan during massive live-fire drills, surrounding the island with warships, aircraft and military pressure as tensions rise. (PLA Eastern Theater Command via Reuters)
Clark said the Army now has more resources committed to the region than at any previous point in his career, including additional divisions, a corps headquarters and specialized formations designed to conduct long-range strikes and operations across multiple domains.
"The Army is now better resourced in the Pacific than I've ever seen it," he said.
He pointed to the Army's growing ability to support naval and air operations, including land-based weapons capable of striking targets at sea.
Clark said recent military war games have demonstrated the importance of those capabilities, including one maritime scenario in which the addition of Army forces changed an unfavorable outcome.
"It's really tied to existing capabilities we have," Clark said, citing the Army's ability to detect targets, conduct strikes, protect military assets and sustain operations from land.

items.title: Germany shifts toward tougher EU trade defenses as pressure from Chinese competition grows - DW.com
items.summary: <a href="https://news.google.
items.content:
Germany and France are pushing for stronger EU trade defense tools amid rising Chinese competition Image: DW Advertisement
Germany's cautious approach toward Beijing is cracking. For years, Berlin blocked a harder line on what the European Union describes as China's   unfair trade practices.
In the last few months, that caution — a fear of Chinese retaliation that could hurt  German exporters — has given way to a willingness to escalate.
Last week, Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron wrote jointly to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen seeking a new tool to cut a trading partner off from the EU's single market  if unfair practices continue.
Clearly aimed at Beijing, the letter warned the measure was necessary against countries that "deliberately seek to undermine ... fair market conditions by political or economic means." 
China's Commerce Ministry warned Europe would "suffer the consequences" if it adopted such a "kill-switch" plan, which was timed to coincide with crucial EU-China trade talks in Beijing last week.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Noah Barkin, a senior adviser with research consultancy Rhodium Group's China practice, told DW that the threats to Germany's export powerhouse "have convinced Merz and his closest advisers that the benefits of action outweigh the costs of inaction." 
Before the COVID pandemic , the two economies rose in tandem and German industry benefited from China's ascent .
Since 2021, however, China has fallen from Germany's second-largest export market to its ninth, according to data from Germany Trade & Invest for the first half of 2026.
Chinese competitors have quickly closed the technology gap and benefit from much lower costs and state subsidies. That pressure is being felt especially in Germany's automaking , precision engineering and chemicals industries.
German vehicle makers have suffered a large sales drop in China, which was once their second-largest market. According to data from Rhodium Group, German car exports to China plummeted by 66% between 2022 and 2025.
Big German brands now face heavy rivalry from a new wave of Chinese electric vehicle (EV) manufactures in other major markets, including Europe, which is forcing a wave of  layoffs and possible factory closures .
VW, Audi and Porsche have announced workforce reductions totaling tens of thousands of jobs as the industry undergoes a huge transformation Image: Sven Hoppe/dpa/picture alliance
In Germany alone, imports of new Chinese-made cars rose 121% in the first seven months of the year, according to Destatis, the federal statistics agency. Overall, Chinese-made vehicles accounted for nearly 14% of total vehicle imports.
"After continuously losing market share in China ... it [the rivalry] seems to be hitting their business within the European automotive market," Andreas Mischer, an associate fellow at the Berlin-based Mercator Institute for China Studies (MERICS), told DW.
Mischer said pressure from Germany's powerful automotive lobby was key to Berlin's "shifting attitude toward trade defense instruments."
Among the many German business leaders who have demanded a more hard-line approach in recent months, Oliver Richtberg, head of foreign trade at VDMA, Germany's mechanical engineering association, was perhaps the most blunt:
"We are currently being deindustrialized through unfair measures — and most companies are no longer willing to accept this," Richtberg told Welt am Sonntag newspaper in August.
According to Eurostat, the wider EU's goods deficit with China was around €360 billion ($402 billion) last year — effectively €1 billion per day — and widened again in the first half of 2026.
While Brussels has been pushing back against the dumping of cheap Chinese goods, a separate industrial protection law and other anti-coercion measures are running into trouble from Beijing and at home.
Business groups question industrial policy proposals
The EU's Industrial Accelerator Act, proposed in March, aims to pull manufacturing investment back to Europe by favoring EU-based firms in public contracts and subsidies.
Foreign investments in key sectors would only be approved if European partners keep majority control, which Beijing has framed as discriminatory.
How to dismantle China's stranglehold on raw materials?
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
The European Automobile Manufacturers' Association (ACEA) warned last month that the draft act does little to counter the threat from cheaper Chinese rivals. In a position paper, it said the incentive to produce within the bloc has to be large enough to "cancel out the extra cost of producing locally."
Berlin's chief concern was that China could place new export curbs on rare earth minerals and the magnets made from them. China has a stranglehold on these elements, which are essential for German automotive, renewables and defense manufacturing.
Bloomberg last week cited unnamed German officials as saying that a new EU kill-switch could be a "second-strike weapon" if Beijing blocked those exports. Brussels is also considering unilateral limits on how many hybrid cars China can export to the EU, according to the same Bloomberg report. 
Perhaps to avoid such an open confrontation, the EU and China reached a "shared understanding" last week at the EU-China trade talks in Beijing that could cut Chinese exports of hybrid and plug-in hybrid vehicles to the European Union by more than half, according to EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic, who headed the European delegation.
Reports say the agreement would cap such Chinese imports at 350,000 vehicles annually, with the limit increasing by 6% each year over four years.
Amid intense Chinese rivalry, the EU says it wants to restore industrial production in Europe Image: Torsten Krüger/imageBROKER/picture alliance Overall, new hybrid-electric cars in the EU reached nearly 37% of all new cars registered from January to August, according to ACEA data.
MERICS, meanwhile, calculated that the EU is a more critical export market for China than the US. In the first half of the year, Chinese exports to the EU were $254 billion (€354 billion), versus $172 billion to the US.
This could give EU negotiators a firmer hand as they seek to avoid a trade war while protecting Europe from China's latest export glut.
"The EU has more leverage than it sometimes thinks," MERICS' Mischer told DW.

items.title: How Trump’s tariffs and Iran war are becoming liabilities in Michigan’s Senate race
items.summary: Republicans are largely leaving Trump out of general election ads, with some battleground candidates breaking from him on tariffs and Iran.
items.content:
Mike Rogers breaks with Trump in Michigan Senate race on tariffs, Iran
Michigan Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers is distancing himself from President Donald Trump on tariffs and the Iran war as economic concerns dominate the battleground race.
Republican candidates are largely leaving Trump out of their general election ads after leaning heavily on him in the primaries, with just 4.3% mentioning him now, down from 47.1%, according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data.
The Michigan contest could help decide control of the Senate, making Rogers’ effort to hold Trump’s base while appealing to swing voters a key test for the GOP.
Michigan Republican Senate candidate, former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers speaks during a barn party campaign event at Hoffman Farms Winery on Oct. 9, 2026 in Highland Township, Michigan.
Michigan Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers sat at a neighborhood bar, a bottle of Canadian Labatt Blue pilsner in hand, and delivered a message that would have been hard to imagine just weeks ago.
"Here in Michigan, we know that Canada is not our enemy," Rogers says into the camera in an advertisement released Oct. 7. "We need to end this tariff war now."
He never mentions the man who started it: President Donald Trump .
It's a dramatic reversal for Rogers, who spent months defending Trump's tariffs , saying as recently as September that " Trump is right to put America first " by imposing duties. But in Michigan, where farms, factories and tourism rely on Canadian trade, Trump's trade fight and Ottawa's retaliation have become a political quagmire three weeks before an election that could decide Senate control.
Rogers is locked in a dead heat with Democrat Abdul El-Sayed . The Cook Political Report with Amy Walter rates the contest a toss-up, with neither candidate emerging as a clear favorite. Polling aggregator FiftyPlusOne has El-Sayed with a four-percentage-point advantage over Rogers.
And Rogers' omission of Trump – mirrored in an earlier ad calling for an end to the war in Iran – reflects broader GOP anxiety heading into November's election. Even as Trump urges voters to " pretend I'm on the ballot ," many battleground Republicans are barely talking about him in general election ads, with some using them to tacitly break with his signature policies.
Fifty-seven of 1,324 Republican candidate ads in the general election period mention Trump – 4.3%, down from 47.1% during the primaries, according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data. The analysis counts distinct ads, rather than how often they aired, and includes spots scheduled through the end of October.
Democratic candidates are invoking Trump far more often. He appears in 20.9% of their general election ads, nearly five times the Republican rate.
"Republicans needed to toe the Trump line to win the base in the primaries, but they need independence to survive November," said Ron Bonjean , a Republican strategist and partner at ROKK Solutions.
Michigan conducts roughly $80 billion in annual trade with Ontario, according to the Michigan Chamber of Commerce. Canada is also Michigan's top export market, buying $23.2 billion in goods last year, roughly 39% of all state exports, according to the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative.
The relationship is especially important to automakers , whose parts routinely crisscross the border before final assembly. The Detroit Three – General Motors , Ford and Stellantis – reported roughly $6.5 billion in combined tariff-related costs in 2025, according to a CNBC analysis of company financial disclosures.
"You can't slap a tariff on goods crossing that bridge without immediately inflating the cost of every vehicle rolling off a Michigan assembly line," said Richard Czuba , founder of the Glengariff Group, a Michigan polling firm.
Trump escalated the trade fight with Canada again in August. After negotiations collapsed, the U.S. imposed 50% tariffs on roughly $20 billion of Canadian goods, hitting steel, aluminum and manufacturing inputs on top of existing duties on lumber and autos. Canada responded with retaliatory tariffs .
The new duties landed as Michigan was already feeling the strain. The state reported Michigan's agricultural exports to Canada fell 12.3% in 2025, while Democratic Gov. Gretchen Whitmer's administration estimated tariffs were averaging Michigan households about $1,000 a year .
"Republicans in tight races like Rogers are largely avoiding Trump's priorities — or breaking with him, especially on tariffs — because the cost of living is such a potent issue," said Erika Franklin Fowler, a Wesleyan University professor and co-director of the Wesleyan Media Project , which tracks political advertising.
An early September WDIV/Detroit News poll by the Glengariff Group found 64.2% of likely Michigan voters opposed Trump's Canadian tariffs, with nearly 62% saying they hurt the state's economy.
Against that backdrop, Rogers pivoted. After calling tariffs " necessary " in late August, he was on the air by October demanding an end to the fight " to lower your prices ."
"Mike Rogers was a free-trade Republican until being a free-trade Republican put him at odds with Trump," Czuba told CNBC. "Now he's coming back to where he started because Michigan voters have made clear how much they dislike the tariffs on Canada."
Rogers' campaign did not respond to requests for comment on his shifts on tariffs and Iran or whether he is seeking greater distance from Trump.
Trump's standing leaves Rogers little room for error in a state the president carried by just 1.4 points in 2024 even as Rogers lost in his earlier bid for the Senate. A September Emerson College/Nexstar Media survey found 55% of likely Michigan voters disapproved of Trump's performance, while 47% cited the economy as their top issue.
That leaves Rogers walking a tightrope: energizing Trump's base while convincing swing voters he can shield them from the economic fallout of the administration's policies.
"When voters feel squeezed at the pump and the grocery store, tariffs and wars abroad are what they will vote on," Bonjean told CNBC. "If a conflict drives up daily costs, battleground candidates have a harder time defending it. This cycle has created a storm."
Rogers initially called Trump's decision to strike Iran " the right thing to do " and hailed the conflict as the best opportunity for Middle East peace in his lifetime. But as the war dragged on and energy costs climbed, his tone changed.
Michigan highway diesel hit $6.71 a gallon in September, while off-road diesel used by farmers reached $5.95 for Sept. 21 delivery, according to Michigan Farm News, a publication of the Michigan Farm Bureau, citing fuel distributor Crystal Flash. Nationally, farm fuel expenses were projected to rise 29% this year, while fertilizer costs were projected to rise 15%, according to a U.S. Department of Agriculture forecast.
By late September, Rogers was calling for a quick end to the war because "Michigan families are struggling with the price of everyday life." Again, Trump's name was missing from the ad.
"Groceries cost too much," he said. "We have to bring prices down."
Former US President and Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump shakes hands with US Senate candidate Mike Rogers, Republican of Michigan, as Rogers takes the stage to speak during a campaign rally at the Suburban Collection Showplace in Novi, Michigan, October 26, 2024.
Rogers' late pivots may make it too late to create daylight after months of alignment with Trump, one GOP strategist said.
"It's a high-wire act with no safety net," Bonjean said. "Voters already have defined impressions of this administration, and suddenly flipping your positions on Trump in the final weeks looks to a lot of people more like self-preservation than an authentic conversion."
Republicans have the money to test the strategy. In September, Republicans spent about $200 million more than Democrats on aired congressional ads — $597 million to $398 million, according to AdImpact .
That advantage extended to Michigan, where Republicans held a $15 million edge in Senate advertising race through Sept. 30, according to AdImpact. Rogers and the National Republican Senatorial Committee had spent $12 million on coordinated ads, according to AdImpact.
Rogers has also tried to move the race onto friendlier ground by attacking El-Sayed over transgender rights.
"Abdul thinks football is bad, but men playing in women's sports is good," Rogers said in an August attack ad . "Common sense versus crazy. That's Michigan's choice."
About one in nine ads run by Rogers' campaign, the NRSC and their coordinated operation since the primary have addressed transgender issues, accounting for nearly $800,000 of $14.4 million in Michigan Senate ad spending scheduled through the end of October, according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data.
Nationally, anti-transgender messaging accounted for nearly a fifth of pro-GOP Senate broadcast ads from Sept. 8-27, according to the Wesleyan Media Project, trailing only taxes and inflation. A Reuters/Ipsos survey found 67% of Americans support barring transgender girls and women from female school sports.
"Republicans are looking for any way to distract from the economy," said Meredith Kelly , a Democratic strategist and partner at Declaration Media. "They are not popular when it comes to pocketbook issues like gas, groceries and healthcare costs."
El-Sayed has largely declined to engage on transgender issues, instead steering the conversation back to affordability. But when pressed, he has said decisions over gender-affirming care for minors should be left to patients, parents and doctors, and told Fox News that sports governing bodies should set eligibility rules.
"You have not asked me one time about the issues that people actually care about in Michigan," El-Sayed told host Jesse Watters, pointing to gas, groceries and prescription costs.
That approach puts El-Sayed in one camp of a Democratic debate left unresolved after 2024: whether to directly rebut Republican attacks on transgender rights, concede ground on specific policies or change the subject.
El-Sayed's campaign did not respond to a request for comment on its strategy for responding to the Republican attacks. El-Sayed will get a high-profile boost from Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., who is set to campaign with him across Michigan on Thursday and hold additional rallies around Detroit on Friday.
Meanwhile, some Democrats have moved right. In neighboring Ohio , longtime Democratic Rep. Marcy Kaptur recently ran an ad declaring that "boys should not play in girls' sports," angering LGBTQ+ advocates and some party allies. Others argue that engaging only gives Republicans the culture war they want.
"There isn't one playbook, and it's different across the country," Kelly told CNBC.
There is evidence, however, that silence carries a cost. A Democratic post-election autopsy found attacks on former Vice President Kamala Harris over social issues were " very effective " in 2024. Subsequent testing by the centrist think tank Third Way found that not responding cost Democrats roughly eight points, a penalty largely erased by a direct rebuttal.
"You cannot just hit mute when Republicans launch a cultural attack," said Lanae Erickson , senior vice president for social policy, education and politics at centrist think tank Third Way. "Changing the subject doesn't defuse the issue; it gives Republicans free rein to define you."
Yet in Michigan, analysts say the economy may make it difficult for any cultural issue to dominate the closing weeks.
"If Rogers wants to bet on cultural grievances to drown out economic pain, that's a huge gamble," Czuba said. "You can talk about sports all day, but when swing voters are paying six dollars for diesel, it's going to be hard to beat kitchen table issues."

items.content:
Figure caption, Watch: Why the lonely in China are hiring 'temporary children'
"The biggest difficulty really was the loneliness. Sometimes, if I wanted to talk to someone I'd talk to the TV."
Yang, 91, lives on the outskirts of China's bustling capital Beijing. Following the death of her husband, she was so lonely that she says she even considered the possibility of voluntary euthanasia.
"I asked my son about it but he told me it was banned. I told him that if it ever becomes legal I want to do it - I didn't want to live any longer."
Suffering glaucoma, with failing eyesight, she was unable to even do basic things like adjust the controls on her air conditioner.
Cases such as Yang's have become increasingly common in Chinese cities which Associate Professor Teresa Kuan, from the Chinese University of Hong Kong, says is "exacerbated by the structure of society and the modes by which people interact".
There are many causes of isolation in China. Like when rural migrants pursue economic opportunities, leaving behind close-knit support networks for urban centres where loneliness and uncertainty can be difficult to overcome, or when graduates uproot themselves chasing employment on the other side of the country.
Image caption, Suffering from glaucoma and failing eyesight, 91-year-old Yang found simple tasks and daily life increasingly difficult on her own.
But now a growing "loneliness industry" has emerged to try to fill these gaps in people's lives.
Yang says her life has been transformed by one of these services - Wang Yingwei and his electric scooter delivery team - who started coming over twice a day with hot meals but whose help extends far beyond that.
"We see ourselves as community children," Yingwei told the BBC. "It means putting yourself in the shoes of older people and carefully considering their needs.
"For example, they may be drinking tap water which can be cloudy and contain a lot of lime. I can fix this problem with a filtered water tank. Such a small thing can make them much happier. Maybe they can't shower because their equipment is broken. I'll buy a part, replace it and their shower is fine."
"The elderly treat us like their children, and we treat them like our own parents," he added.
Yingwei's services cost less than half the price of employing a caregiver.
Image caption, Wang Yingwei and his small delivery team offer more than just meals, bringing human connection to elderly residents.
The former mobile phone salesman says he started his company to help seniors remain at home without having to move into retirement facilities. He was inspired to do this after his own father-in-law, who had developed Alzheimer's, had to go into a nursing home. Yingwei said he felt that the conditions there were so sub-standard he wanted to make sure others could stay out of institutions like this for as long as possible.
His small business currently employs four people but he says there is a possibility he will expand as demand grows.
There is still a shortage of solid data on the size of this sector â which operators say has exploded in recent years â but securities company Sinolink valued it at around $7.4 billion in 2025. And this is only expected to grow given the trajectory of modern lifestyles.
Zheng Ruizhi, another client of Yingwei's who lives in Beijing's northern outskirts, welcomed him at the door with a big smile.
"After retiring, I don't have much opportunity to hang out with others," the 75-year-old, whose son lives two hours away from her, told the BBC.
She was recovering from a recent injury which she said was making everyday tasks more difficult.
Image caption, Zheng Ruizhi, 75, shares a lighthearted moment with Wang Yingwei during a home visit.
But the arrival of Yingwei â who she calls her "dear boy" â lightened her mood.
"I call you 'dear boy' because I am so fond of you. I genuinely like you from the bottom of my heart. I also admire and trust you. When you help me out, I don't have a single worry or fear," she told him.
Yet the services offered by those in this sector are not limited to home visits.
Twenty-three-year-old Liu Yanyan, for instance, works as a "medical escort". She acts as a friendly face taking clients to see the doctor, or picking up their test results or medication from city hospitals, which can be intimidatingly large and bureaucratic.
"Some of my customers are people in their 20s who came to Beijing to build a career. They might not have friends here or feel awkward asking colleagues to accompany them because of the concept of social reciprocity in Chinese culture," she said. "If I accompanied you to a doctor's appointment for free, you might feel obligated to buy me a meal or a movie ticket afterwards."
She said that, because of this, there are many people in modern Chinese society who tend to keep to themselves.
"So, they hire someone like me to accompany them to the hospital. If they had to go alone, they could feel scared or anxious."
Image caption, Liu Yanyan, a 23-year-old medical escort, helps clients navigate complex city hospitals.
At the core of many businesses catering to loneliness in China is a simple offering: human connection.
Teresa Kuan said that some people prefer the option of pouring their hearts out to a complete stranger for a fee.
"If there is a companion you have paid for, the relationship is not exactly equal. It is a service relationship, so you don't have to deal with the unpredictability of a standard relationship. The thing about friendship is that it can be unpredictable. You don't know when someone might disappoint you. But, in a service relationship, you have a better idea of what to expect."
Wang Zhoutao runs a hiking business to help people who want to climb China's famous mountain Huangshan in Anhui Province.
"We provide emotional support, like cheering them up, taking their photo or telling jokes. It's really a service based on companionship," he said.
The former soldier added that he normally hikes up the mountain with clients 10 to 15 days a month. When fully booked, this could be as many as 30 times a month.
Image caption, Mountain escort Wang Zhoutao guides a client up the steep steps of Mount Huangshan.
He gave an example of a young woman he once accompanied who felt ostracised at work. "She felt useless and wanted to prove something to herself," he said.
"We started climbing but it was a tough trek as the weather was really hot and we were sweating a lot. There were moments she wanted to give up but I told her, 'If you quit now and can't get over this mountain how will you handle anything else in life?'. I kept encouraging her."
After they made it all the way he said she sent him a long message of thanks describing her inner journey and expressing her gratitude.
"The pace of life is just too fast these days. People face pressure from work, relationships and family expectations," he said. "I think my clients are mostly people who feel a void in their relationships or have suffered a setback."
Human connection is a necessity but, in a society grappling with loneliness across generations, it has now also become a commodity.
Back in her little Beijing flat, Yang is feeling more comfortable now that Yingwei has sorted out her problem of making the air conditioner work properly.
"It's good to have someone around when you need it, someone you can share your innermost thoughts with," she said.
"I did struggle with loneliness but that's been resolved now. I'm quite happy.
"I can't lose Yingwei and the others. They've all got a good heart."

Qnity Bets On Local Production To Win More AI Chip Business From Nvidia, TSMC – CEO Touts ‘Local-For-Local’ Strategy
Qnity is reportedly using a local-for-local sourcing strategy to strengthen supply chains, respond faster to customers, and compete for more business from major chipmakers.
The close-up view of a CPU socket on a computer motherboard. (Photo by Narumon Bowonkitwanchaivia via Getty Images)
CEO Jon Kemp said materials innovation is becoming increasingly important to the AI industry as demand grows for advanced chips and supporting technologies.
In an interview with Nikkei Asia, Qnity CEO said the company sources more than 70% of its raw materials within the regions where it operates.
He added that the firm is expanding production capacity across Asia and the U.S.
Qnity (Q), a key supplier of semiconductor materials to Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. (TSM) and Intel (INTC), is reportedly betting that local production and sourcing will help it win more business from chipmakers.
The strategy comes amid rising demand for materials used throughout the AI chip supply chain, including in technologies developed by Nvidia (NVDA).
CEO Jon Kemp told Nikkei Asia Qnity’s “local-for-local” strategy, which involves sourcing more than 70% of its raw materials within the regions where it operates, helps the company respond faster to customers, strengthen supply chains, and win a role in developing advanced chip technologies.
“Our belief in that local-for-local operating model and being that partner of choice is to allow us to accelerate the pace of innovation and match the speed of our customers,” Kemp said.
Q stock edged as much as 1% lower in pre-market trade, on track to extend a drop of over 6% over the past five days. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around Qnity slipped to ‘bearish’ from ‘neutral’ territory over the past day.
Qnity’s strategy reflects a broader shift in the semiconductor industry, the report said.
Tariffs, industrial policy and concern about production concentrated in Taiwan are pushing chipmakers and suppliers to build closer to customers.
The U.S. imposed Section 232 chip tariffs in January and signed a reshoring deal with Taiwan the following day. TSMC is  expanding in Arizona, and GlobalFoundries last week  agreed to make interposers for TSMC in New York.
For Qnity, Kemp said the company’s manufacturing footprint and regional sourcing model give it an advantage by improving supply chain resilience, creating new business opportunities, and reducing exposure to logistics-driven inflation.
Qnity recently invested $61.5 million to expand production capacity for advanced semiconductor materials and chemicals in Taiwan. It is also expanding in South Korea and has doubled its capacity in Vietnam.
In the U.S., the company opened a facility in Delaware earlier this year to support growing domestic production of advanced processors and memory chips.
Qnity supplies semiconductor chemicals and materials to major chipmakers, including TSMC, Samsung and Intel. Its portfolio includes chemical mechanical polishing (CMP) pads and slurries, plus materials for advanced chip packaging and thermal management.
Kemp said Qnity’s CMP-related business grew 20% in 2026. Materials for advanced packaging, AI-related printed circuit boards and thermal management applications each grew more than 50% year over year in the first half of the year.
“Materials are moving kind of from backstage to center stage,” Kemp said. “Materials innovation is a hidden hero of the AI era.”
In pre-market trade,  TSM stock fell nearly 1% while  INTC stock was down as much as 1.5%. Meanwhile,  NVDA stock shed more than 1% amid  broader weakness in semiconductor stocks. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around NVDA and INTC continued to trend in ‘bearish’ territory over the past day. Sentiment around TSM deteriorated to ‘neutral’ from the ‘bullish’ zone.
Qnity is scheduled to report its third-quarter (Q3) earnings results on November 4. Investors will be watching whether growth converts to free cash flow under incoming CFO Ken Rizvi. The company guided to $600 million to $700 million in free cash flow this year.
The market is expecting the firm to report earnings per share (EPS) of $1.20, on revenue of $1.49B, according to Koyfin data.

By Joanne Clark · Wednesday, October 14, 2026 · 1 min read

In a statement, the government said it rejected the measures announced by China’s Foreign Ministry on October 12, describing them as unwarranted and reaffirming Belize’s right to determine its foreign policy without external pressure.
China accused Fonseca and a senior government minister in Paraguay of pursuing “anti-China” policies by supporting continued diplomatic ties with Taiwan.
The measures include denying the two officials entry to Hong Kong and Macau and prohibiting Chinese organizations and individuals from engaging in transactions or other activities with them.

items.title: Saudi employee charged with planting recording device in OpenAI office
items.summary: Prosecutors say the device, wrapped in toilet paper, was found inserted in a USB port on the back of a TV in an executive conference room.
items.content:
Image caption, Prosecutors released CCTV images of the suspect allegedly checking on the secret recorder
A Saudi national has been charged with secretly planting a recording device in one of OpenAI's offices in California, federal prosecutors announced.
Abdulrahman Alfozan, who worked at the AI firm as an engineer, was charged federally with using or endeavouring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications.
OpenAI said it had discovered a "sophisticated recording device" hidden in their San Francisco office and alerted the FBI. The company said it used its AI models to track that it had been planted by an employee.
Prosecutors say the device, wrapped in toilet paper, was found inserted in a USB port on the back of a TV in an executive conference room.
OpenAI, the maker of the popular chatbot ChatGPT, said that it has no indication that source code, model weights or customer data were inappropriately accessed or taken in the incident. It said the employee has been fired.
According to the complaint, Alfozan "allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer's executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications," FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement.
Patel said that the alleged goal was to capture information about the company's AI product.
Alfozan has been working as an engineer at OpenAI since July 2025, prosecutors say.
On 30 September, OpenAI employees discovered the device - two days after prosecutors say it had been installed. The device was encrypted, prosecutors said.
OpenAI said they were able to use their AI models "to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier".
According to the FBI, the suspect used a "productivity tool" and a "chatbot" to research sensitive locations at OpenAI and how to secretly place audio equipment.
Chatbot prompts that he is alleged to have searched include "building, customising, installing, audio recording, testing, obfuscating, and remote accessing a device", prosecutors allege.
He is also accused of using the chatbot to ask about "'build[ing] a continuous audio recorder,' 'customis[ing] Wi-Fi . . . connectivity,' 'improv[ing] audio and live listening,' and 'encrypt[ing] the SD card'".
Image caption, The device was allegedly concealed in toilet paper
On 5 October, prosecutors say he allegedly returned to inspect the device in the office room. Prosecutors used CCTV camera footage to link him to the scene.
That same day, Alfozan left a bag unattended in a different part of the building. A security team for OpenAI opened it to find his wallet and ID, as well as another recording device that was similar to the one found in the office conference room, prosecutors said.
Alfozan appeared in court on Tuesday. It's unclear whether he has legal representation.
If found guilty, he faces up to five years in prison and a fine of $250,000 (Â£187,000).

LONDON -- At least 600,000 people were without power early Wednesday in Ukraine, after Russia launched an aerial attack that struck energy infrastructure, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
"A targeted Russian ballistic missile strike specifically against energy infrastructure -- the very infrastructure covered by the ceasefire announced by the American President," the Ukrainian president said on social media.
Victoria Deineko holds her daughter Mia while standing in front of a multi-story residential building damaged in a Russian missile strike in Kyiv, Ukraine, Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026.
President Donald Trump said on Sunday that both sides had agreed to an "energy ceasefire."
The outages on Wednesday may become more widespread, the president said, as there is "significant" damage to at least 26 power facilities and four others in the gas and oil sector.
The attack included some 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 drones, officials said, with many targeted Kyiv and its surrounding area.

Katarina Mathernova, the European Union's ambassador to Ukraine, said more than a dozen explosions were heard before dawn in the Kyiv.
"A nine-storey apartment building was hit in the capital. Fire spread through people’s homes," Mathernova said early on Wednesday. "Rescuers helped residents down ladders while others stood outside, watching their building burn."

Tech Bytes: Microsoft ramps up AI chip challenge as Google and Apple push deeper into AI
Tech Bytes: Microsoft ramps up AI chip challenge as Google and Apple push deeper into AI Proactive uses images sourced from Shutterstock Microsoft is stepping up its challenge to Nvidia in the artificial intelligence chip market, while Google and Apple have unveiled major AI products as competition intensifies across chips, software and consumer devices.
The developments highlight an accelerating push by the world's largest technology companies to control more of the AI ecosystem and reduce their dependence on outside suppliers.
Microsoft plans to make its internally developed Maia processors the primary AI inference system across its products and services as it expands the technology to multi-gigawatt deployments from 2027.
Its Maia 200 processor is already handling production workloads including Microsoft Copilot, while the next-generation Maia 300 is scheduled to enter service next year.
The Maia 300 can process about 40% more AI tokens per megawatt than leading graphics processing unit-based systems, an important metric as power consumption becomes one of the biggest constraints on AI expansion.
The strategy represents a growing competitive threat to Nvidia, which dominates the market for high-end AI processors but counts Microsoft and other major technology groups among its biggest customers.
Microsoft will continue using Nvidia hardware, but its investment in proprietary chips is part of a broader industry shift as cloud operators attempt to lower costs and gain greater control over their infrastructure.
Google has meanwhile made Gemini 4 Argon broadly available to developers, enterprises and subscribers as competition between frontier AI models continues to accelerate.
The model is designed for complex multi-step workloads spanning software development, finance, legal work, cybersecurity and scientific research.
Gemini 4 Argon can process text, images, audio and video and supports a combined input and output context window of up to one million tokens.
Google is increasingly positioning its AI systems to perform longer and more complex workflows rather than simply respond to individual prompts, reflecting the wider industry push towards autonomous AI agents.
Argon is being made available through Google's Gemini platform, developer tools and Antigravity agentic development environment.
Apple has expanded its AI strategy beyond phones and computers with the launch of HomeView, a new seven-inch smart display powered by Apple Intelligence and Siri AI.
HomeView combines entertainment, communications and smart-home controls, allowing users to manage cameras, lighting, thermostats, locks and other connected devices.
The device can recognise up to six people and provide personalised information and controls for individual users.
Apple has also unveiled a new Apple TV 4K powered by Siri AI, a second-generation HomePod mini and a collection of smart-home products developed with companies including LG Electronics and Schneider Electric.
HomeView pre-orders have opened ahead of availability from November 13, including in Australia.
The latest announcements show the AI race increasingly extending across the entire technology stack.
Microsoft is targeting the computing infrastructure underneath AI, Google is pushing increasingly capable models and autonomous software, while Apple is seeking to put AI directly into more consumer devices.
The shift also increases pressure on Nvidia as major customers invest in their own processors, although demand for its graphics processing units remains substantial as global AI infrastructure continues to expand.
Power supply, semiconductor manufacturing capacity and the cost of building data centres remain key constraints as technology companies commit increasingly large amounts of capital to AI.
For investors, attention is now shifting from which companies can build the most capable AI systems to which can turn that technology and infrastructure spending into sustainable revenue and earnings.

items.summary: Iran's stock market surges despite war, currency crisis, worsening economy  The Jerusalem Post
items.content:
Iran's stock market climbs despite US blockade, energy shortages, collapsing currency
The stock market rebound could mean two things: either investors believe Tehran and Washington will reach a peace deal soon, or they don’t have any other way to stop their savings from losing value.
Cut off from much of the international banking system, the Central Bank of Iran has increasingly turned to capital controls and foreign-currency restrictions to contain the economic fallout.
Iran’s stock market has recently rallied despite its plummeting economy .
Iran International reported on Tuesday that the Iranian stock market has seen an influx of Investments, despite increasing power outages, a shortage of foreign currency, and the rate of the rial tanking .
The report noted that this could mean one of two things: either investors believe Tehran and Washington will reach a peace deal soon, or they have no other way to stop their savings from losing value.
Iran International points to a few competing analyses of the situation to better explain investors’ choices.
One analysis from Farau indicates that a lack of foreign exchange currency in the country, energy shortages, and uncertainty over the war are the primary stressors for Tehran’s economy.
Vessels transit the Strait of Hormuz off the coast of the port city of Bandar Abbas in southern Iran on September 5, 2026; illustrative (credit: ATTA KENARE / AFP via Getty Images)
Iranian oil exports have effectively stopped under the US blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, leaving Iran with a dwindling supply of foreign currency.
The report noted that Khabar Online cited a 35,000-toman rise ($.003495) in the free-dollar market in the last month alone.
Additionally, energy shortages in Iran are exacerbating the problems. Iran's energy sector was already underfunded before the war began, and strikes on Iranian energy infrastructure have further strained production.
On top of that, Iranian investors are unsure what comes next. The economic effects of a third round of war would be disastrous, but diplomatic efforts continue.
Businesses that rely on imported goods are feeling these effects, as they face higher operating costs with less access to foreign currency, Iran International added.
These factors significantly complicate long-term investment and leave Iranians seeking assets that will preserve their value.
Some analyses indicated that investors are optimistic about a deal.
Rouydad24 argued that investors expect a deal and believe more access to international markets is on the horizon.
However, Iran International noted that other analyses show a different picture.
Just because the market is rising does not mean that investors in Iran are optimistic about the country’s economic prospects. Instead, it might indicate that Iranian’s lack alternatives for preserving their wealth.
The rial’s value has tanked, property is losing value, and bank deposits are losing purchasing power, making domestic equities more attractive to investors, the report noted.
This could offer a more stable assessment than the first: investors may be buying domestic stocks out of fear that cash will lose value in the country.
This comes as the International Monetary Fund forecasted that Iran’s economy would contract by 7.6% in 2026, as compared to the rate of 5.4% projected in July.
Notably, Iran International noted that the Middle East and Central Asia were expected to contract by 0.3%.

Taiwan agrees to buy 30% of gas from Alaska LNG project, Trump says
U.S. President Donald Trump said Taiwan had agreed to buy 30% of the gas from a pipeline project in Alaska.
The terms of the deal remain unclear, though Taiwan's state-owned CPC Corp reached an agreement last year to purchase LNG and invest in the project.
Trump's remarks come amid uncertainty over South Korea's participation in the $50 billion Alaska LNG project, despite his repeated claims that Seoul had agreed to join.
WASILLA, ALASKA - OCTOBER 13: U.S. President Donald Trump speaks during an election rally at the Menard Memorial Sports Center on October 13, 2026 in Wasilla, Alaska. President Trump is in Alaska campaigning for local Republican candidates ahead of the midterm elections. (Photo by Alex Wong/Getty Images)
U.S. President Donald Trump said Tuesday that Taiwan had agreed to buy 30% of the gas from a proposed liquefied natural gas project in Alaska.
"Taiwan has just agreed to buy 30% of the gas coming off the pipeline for the next 20 years," Trump said at a rally in Alaska. "That guarantees a success."
His latest remarks follow repeated claims earlier this month that South Korea had agreed to join the $50 billion Alaska LNG project, even as Seoul maintained that its participation had not been finalized. "We'll also invest $4.4 billion into the project, on top of $50 billion already committed by South Korea to Alaska," Trump said.
However, the terms of the Taiwan deal cited by Trump were not immediately clear.
Last year, Taiwan's state-owned energy company CPC Corp reportedly reached an agreement with Alaska Gasline Development Corp to purchase LNG and invest in the pipeline project.
Taiwan, home to critical semiconductor giant TSMC, has seen energy demand climb due to AI-related growth. However, the island relies on imports for more than 90% of its energy supply and this summer projected its average electricity demand growth rate through 2035 would exceed that of Japan and South Korea.
Taiwan's economic affairs ministry said that growth rate would climb by about 2.5% a year, the second-highest forecast in its history. The democratically self-ruled island is still waiting on major new arms sales from the U.S.
Glenfarne, the developer of the Alaska LNG pipeline, told the U.S. government in a report this month the project aims to deliver its first gas in 2029.
Trump has also stepped up pressure on South Korea over its participation in the project, warning earlier this month that he would charge the country more and threatened to double the charges if Seoul failed to sign soon, without specifying what would be doubled. That prompted speculation in South Korean media that he was referring to higher tariffs.
The White House, Taiwan's energy ministry and CPC Corp. did not immediately respond to CNBC's requests for comment.

On long-term equity returns, Siegel wrote that with the S&P 500 trading around 19 times earnings, the inverse P/E suggests roughly a 5.5% long-term real return, and he raised his estimate of long-term real equity returns to approximately 5.5%–6.5%. He said, “Higher rates are not necessarily bearish for stocks if those rates reflect stronger productivity and economic growth.”
Siegel said equities can continue to move higher if yields stabilize and growth expectations remain intact, and he flagged a risk he is monitoring: “The real danger would be a sudden technological breakthrough that makes a large portion of the current spending on data centers and compute obsolete.” He added, “But there is no evidence of that today.”
