items.title: Closer EU trade ties greater prize for UK than making separate deals, minister says
items.summary: Exclusive: Douglas Alexander, on trade delegation to India, talks up economic benefits of joint trading arrangements with EuropeUK politics live – latest updatesBritain will benefit from much closer trading relations with the EU even if that means giving up its ability to negotiate free trade agreements, the Scotland secretary ha
items.content:
Douglas Alexander visit GSK in Mumbai as part of a trade delegation to India. Photograph: X/Douglas Alexander
Douglas Alexander visit GSK in Mumbai as part of a trade delegation to India. Photograph: X/Douglas Alexander
Closer EU trade ties greater prize for UK than making separate deals, minister says
Exclusive: Douglas Alexander, on trade delegation to India, talks up economic benefits of joint trading arrangements with Europe
Britain will benefit from much closer trading relations with the EU even if that means giving up its ability to negotiate free trade agreements, the Scotland secretary has said.
Douglas Alexander helped negotiate deals with India and the US when he was a trade minister under Keir Starmer.
But he has told the Guardian he thinks joint trading arrangements with the EU – whether under a customs union or full membership – would be a bigger economic prize, not least because the EU has now negotiated its own similar deal with India .
When Starmer was prime minister, ministers would argue against rejoining the EU because it would mean having to abandon trade agreements with other countries.
Douglas Alexander: ‘We’re paying a real economic price for putting up new barriers to our European neighbours.’ Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PA Alexander’s comments show how much Starmer’s successor, Andy Burnham, who called this week for a “serious dialogue” on the UK’s relations with the EU, including possible re-entry, has shifted the government’s position.
Speaking to the Guardian from a trade delegation to India, Alexander welcomed the progress made since the Indian agreement came into force earlier this year, since when the price of scotch whisky in India has fallen by 10-15%.
But he said the economic benefits of trading agreements with the EU would be greater.
“In trade policy, geography still matters,” he said. “The Channel is just 21 miles wide. Our largest trading partner is and will remain the European Union in the years to come. We trade almost twice the amount with the European Union that we do with the United States, the largest single-country trading partner.”
He said: “It’s no secret that I was not a supporter of leaving the European Union, and I called out early as trade minister what I described as the ‘post-imperial delusions’ of the Brexiteers. Back in 2016, they promised a world of Britain as a buccaneering free trade nation in a world where barriers were coming down. Sadly, what we’ve witnessed in the year since is a more protectionist, more regionalised world in which barriers have been going up.
“At the time we joined the Pacific trade grouping, the CPTPP [Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership] – which undoubtedly makes a lot of sense geopolitically for the UK – our own analysis made clear that the long-term boost to UK GDP from membership is less than a tenth of 1%. If you compare that with estimates of the structural damage to the UK economy from Brexit , you get a sense of just how important Europe remains to our future trade and prosperity.
“We’re already paying a real economic price for putting up new barriers to our European neighbours who, with almost half of total UK trade, remain easily our largest trading partners.”
Alexander was speaking in Mumbai, where he was joined by the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, and the environment secretary, Angela Eagle, as well as a group of mayors from northern England. He made it clear he did not support any particular method of achieving closer relations with the EU.
The ministers spent much of their time in meetings with Indian officials as they attempt to iron out what they say have been “teething problems” with the early implementation, especially for smaller businesses.
Keir Starmer and Narendra Modi, India’s prime minister, in Mumbai in October 2025. Photograph: Leon Neal/PA “There are always teething problems,” Alexander said. “We’re also having a conversation at the level of regulation to see how do we overcome non-tariff barriers that can prove to be an inhibitor to the kind of progress we want to see unless they’re addressed.”
Many in the government say a bigger prize will be to reach an agreement at next month’s EU summit, where Burnham hopes to sign new trading deals for emissions, electricity and agricultural products.
One hurdle to delivering that is the UK’s desire to discuss the protectionist “Made in Europe” policy , which British manufacturers fear will shut them out of a key market. EU leaders say they are willing to discuss British entry into that scheme, though they are also pushing for the UK to impose tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles, without which they fear the UK will become a back door into the European market.
Reynolds told the Guardian this week he would not impose tariffs simply because of pressure from Brussels.

items.title: Germany puts Ukrainian on trial accused of blowing up Nord Stream pipelines
items.summary: Four years after the attacks, Serhii Kuznetsov appears in court accused of a plot to destroy Russia's gas pipelines to Germany.
items.content:
Image caption, Serhii Kuznetsov (C) was pictured in court on Wednesday after his anonymity order was lifted
By Jessica Parker ,Â  Berlin correspondent in Hamburg Â  and Â  Paul Kirby ,Â  Europe digital editor
A Ukrainian man has gone on trial in Hamburg accused of blowing up Russia's Nord Stream gas pipelines to Germany, four years after one of the most dramatic acts of sabotage in modern European history.
Prosecutors say Serhii Kuznetsov played a leading role in a team of saboteurs that destroyed the pipelines, accusing him of a war crime. His defence has called for the case to be dismissed.
The case is highly sensitive in Germany, one of Ukraine's closest allies since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, seven months before the attacks took place.
Extradited to Germany last year, Kuznetsov denies the charges, as does a second suspect who is fighting extradition from Croatia.
Kuznetsov became the first suspect to go on trial for the blasts on Wednesday morning, and a packed public gallery looked on as he entered the courtroom, appearing relaxed.
He even smiled at times, including during initial exchanges where he spoke to confirm personal details such as his name and place of birth.
He had previously only been identified by German prosecutors as Serhii K and pictured with his face blurred, before the court lifted an anonymity order on Wednesday.
Kuznetsov, 50, wore a pair of headphones and appeared to listen intently to a translation of proceedings in Ukrainian, as the prosecution read out the charges against him of ordering divers and an explosive expert to attack civilian infrastructure.
The defence outlined their case, telling the court that only circumstantial evidence had emerged in the four years since the Nord Stream blasts.
"[Prosecutors] made a thorough investigation of four years," Italian defence lawyer Nicola Canestrini told the BBC outside the courtroom. "They did not find one single witness, they did not find no forensics, no DNA, no fingerprints - nothing!"
Image caption, Kuznetsov was extradited to Germany from Italy late last year
Canestrini and his colleagues argued that as a soldier the defendant was bound to secrecy, and therefore he could not have a fair trial as he was unable to defend himself.
"Let's say he has an alibi, he was on another secret operation, how can you prove that if he's [not able] to tell us as defence attorneys where he was and which witnesses we could summon?"
Prosecutors argue the case falls under Germany's code of crimes against international law as a war crime, as an "attack by military means against civilian objects".
The defence told the court his extradition to Germany was flawed as no mention had been made at the time of the war crime allegation.
In the months after explosives destroyed three of the four gas pipelines in the Baltic Sea off the island of Bornholm on 26 September 2022, Western suspicion looked towards Moscow without directly apportioning blame.
Russia had already shut off the flow of gas to Germany in Nord Stream 1 weeks before the attack, and Nord Stream 2 had never been turned on. Berlin had frozen the multi-billion dollar project shortly before the invasion and there were reports of suspicious Russian naval movements before the blasts.
As investigators from Sweden, Denmark and Germany tried to find out who carried out the attack, Russia's Vladimir Putin accused the US and its UK allies, blaming "the Anglo-Saxons" - which they denied.
Eventually, after Denmark and Sweden shut down their inquiries, German prosecutors focused on a group of deep-sea divers who had rented a yacht called the Andromeda in the northern German port of Rostock.
They said later that "traces of subsea explosives were found in the samples taken from the boat".
Despite the strain on relations with Kyiv, German prosecutors pressed ahead with the case, and in January 2025 the German federal court of justice ruled that it fell within German territorial jurisdiction , external and prosecutors had a responsibility to act as it involved "undermining [Germany's] internal security".
Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky has always maintained that Ukraine had "nothing to do with [the Nord Stream blasts]", although in their indictment German prosecutors allege the saboteurs conceived the plot "acting by order of Ukrainian state agencies".
Nord Stream trial: How German police followed the evidence - to Ukraine
The case has highlighted differences of opinion on the trial in Kyiv and Berlin.
Oleksandr Merezhko, who chairs the Foreign Affairs Committee in the Ukrainian parliament, points out that the blasts took place during a time of war with Russia and "Nord Stream 2 was nothing but a tool used by Russia in order to get prepared for the war".
He told the BBC they had no confirmation of the German account: "It's one of the versions."
However, Stefan Meister, of the German Council on Foreign Relations, says successive chancellors in Berlin have done their best to remove the politics from the case.
"They tried to make not a big story out of it, not to give it too much attention, to give it to the institutions, to the judiciary that they will deal with it. This is not a political case. So they tried to depoliticise it," he explained.
Image caption, Three of the four Nord Stream pipelines were ruptured by explosions in September 2022
In August 2025, Kuznetsov was arrested after checking into a hotel near the Italian Adriatic resort of Rimini, by police acting under a European arrest warrant issued by federal prosecutors in Germany.
After several weeks of court battles fighting extradition, when his surname emerged in court documents, Kuznetsov was transferred to Germany late last year.
German prosecutors allege that in 2022 he was a serving officer in the Ukrainian army , external , and he had led a group of professional divers, a boat captain and an explosives expert.
While his legal fight was going on in Italy, another Ukrainian man called Volodymyr Zhuravlov successfully challenged Germany's extradition bid in a Polish court.
In a ruling very different from Italy's Supreme Court, the Polish judge ordered Zhuravlov's release in October 2025, stating that the attack on the pipelines was not unlawful, and if Ukraine had organised an armed mission it was "justified, rational and just".
Although he was released by the court in Warsaw, he was arrested last August in Croatia on suspicion of being a suspect who "participated in the dives necessary" for the sabotage.
Last month, Croatia approved his extradition, although it is not clear when that will happen, and if his case could become part of the Hamburg trial.
Despite the difficult nature of the case for Kyiv and Berlin, Ukrainian MP Oleksandr Merezhko does not believe it will spoil relations as "it's in the best national interests of Germany to continue to support us".

items.content:
US Inflation Hits 3.7%, Sinking Bitcoin and Gold: Will the Fed Hike in October?
US consumer prices rose 3.7% in the year to September, above the 3.6% forecast, and Bitcoin and gold fell within minutes. The hotter reading raises the odds of another Federal Reserve rate hike, which would lift borrowing costs.
Core inflation, which strips out volatile food and energy prices, also beat forecasts at 2.6%, against an expected 2.5%. Both measures climbed from August's readings of 3.4% and 2.4%.
Bitcoin (BTC) dropped from about $83,860 to as low as $82,731 in the five minutes after the 8:30 a.m. ET release, Binance data on TradingView shows. It then steadied near $83,125.
Gold fell from $4,153 to $4,117 an ounce in the same window.
US CPI Bitcoin and gold price reaction, 5-minute chart. Source: TradingView "In response to hotter-than-expected inflation data, gold & silver are following bond prices lower. But inflation will keep heating up as the Fed stays behind the curve. This is bullish for precious metals. When inflation rises faster than nominal rates, real interest rates fall," Peter Schiff commented.
Higher rates tend to pull money away from assets that pay no interest, such as gold, and riskier bets like crypto. The US dollar already sits near an 18-month high.
The Consumer Price Index (CPI) tracks what households pay for everyday goods and services. The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) publishes it every month. In August, gasoline cost 27.4% more than a year earlier, BLS data shows.
Core inflation shows whether rising prices are spreading beyond fuel and groceries. That is the measure the Federal Reserve watches most closely when setting interest rates.
The Fed raised its benchmark rate by a quarter point in September, to a range of 3.75% to 4.00%, according to its statement.
September's report was the last major inflation reading before the Fed meets on October 27 and 28. Before the release, rate futures pointed to a hike in December rather than October.
New York Fed President John Williams said this week he still expects one more rate hike before the year ends.
Whether the Fed moves in October or waits until December now sets the cost of money for borrowers, savers, and investors heading into 2027.

A Singapore-flagged container ship has sunk near the Strait of Hormuz after being hit by a projectile, while a separate dry bulk carrier damaged in an earlier attack is also reported to be sinking, maritime security sources said on Wednesday.
The GFS Pride container ship, with a small 2,824 TEU (20-ft equivalent unit) capacity, is "reported sunk with floating containers ... mariners cautioned," the Hydrographer of Pakistan said in a navigational warning to ships dated October 14.
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards Navy, previously said the vessel, carrying more than 2,500 containers, had attempted to transit what it described as an “unauthorised and dangerous” route. The ship caught fire after hitting a naval mine and has sunk in the south of the Strait.
It comes as the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) received a report of an incident where a container ship was struck by an unknown projectile - although it is currently unclear whether the two incidents are linked.
In a statement, Iran’s Guards have warned local vessels and fishermen to take care.
The vessel's United Arab Emirates-based manager GFS Ship Management FZE could not be immediately reached for comment.
The loss of the GFS Pride marks the second vessel to sink since the US-Iran war began on February 28, according to data from UN shipping agency, the International Maritime Organization.
In a separate incident, the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged Cape Dao was reported to be sinking close to the strait after being struck by a projectile on September 23, the sources added.
"The Antigua & Barbuda flagged bulk carrier CAPE DAO, originally hit on the 23 September, is reported to be sinking after an unsuccessful rescue attempt," British maritime risk management group Vanguard said in a note on Wednesday.
Earlier on Wednesday, Iranian news agency Tasnim reported that three fishermen were injured after a fishing boat was struck in an incident involving an unidentified drone near Sirik in southern Iran's Hormozgan province.
It was described as an attack by a US drone, although Iranian authorities have not officially confirmed the circumstances of the incident or who was responsible.
Before the war on Iran , around 125 to 140 large commercial vessels including oil tankers, gas carriers, bunkers and container ships passed through the Strait of Hormuz every day. This came to an effective standstill on February 28, when the United States and Israel launched coordinated military airstrikes across Iran.
While traffic on the 24-mile Strait appeared to be increasing over recent months, two senior Iranian officials say that Iran is deploying new tactics to target ships sailing through the passage as it seeks to keep oil prices high and influence the US midterm elections .
“The aim is to frustrate efforts by the United States and its allies to bring down global oil prices,” one of the two officials said.
But the US military’s Central Command rejects suggestions that Iran is controlling the strait, saying in a post on X on Tuesday: “IRGC's navy commander has no navy. American forces and regional partners clearly control the Strait of Hormuz. Just yesterday U.S. forces assisted Gulf partners in shipping more than 19 million barrels of crude oil through the strait.”
A vessel transits the Gulf of Oman off the coast of Khor Fakkan in the emirate of Sharjah in the east of the UAE. ( AFP/Getty )
As part of the new strategy, Tehran will expand the geographical scope of its operations beyond the Strait of Hormuz to the Gulf of Oman and waters further afield, the officials said.
Analysis by maritime security sources based on attacks reported to UKMTO and maritime security companies in the region suggest this may already be happening. They show Iran targeting ships in areas beyond the Strait of Hormuz, including waters off the coast of Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, in recent days.
The second Iranian official added that Tehran would not allow Trump to bring down oil prices before the November elections.
“Just when they think they are getting close to the point where prices will fall, we will push them away from it. This is a game of chess,” the second official said. “Such vessels would be safe nowhere, even outside the Strait of Hormuz.”
Trump, meanwhile, has continued his threats against Iran, warning Washington will decide its next move “very soon” and describing it as a “failed country” in comments outside the White House on Tuesday.
“They have no economy… they have no money,” he said. “We’ll make a decision on Iran very soon.”
He later said at a campaign rally: “Wait till you see what we do to Iran. We’re going to do a number… wait till you see what we do to Iran, because we’ve sort of had it. The big thing is, they’re not going to have a nuclear weapon. That’s buried under thousands of tonnes of rock.”

The road from Mount Pleasant to Stanley on the Falkland Islands. Photograph: Sean Smith/The Guardian
UK asks Interpol to reject Argentina’s ‘politically motivated’ requests for Falklands oil arrests
Exclusive: Caution urged over Javier Milei government’s ‘red notice’ requests for arrest of individuals linked to oil project
Britain has appealed to Interpol to reject Argentina’s requests for the arrest of individuals involved in a large oil project off the Falkland Islands .
With tensions over the sovereignty of the British overseas territory reaching levels not seen since the war with Argentina in 1982, UK officials have sought urgent assurances from the international organisation.
A letter has been sent to Interpol’s headquarters in Lyon arguing that “red notice” requests from Argentina for the arrest of such individuals, including British nationals, should be seen as politically motivated.
It is understood the UK government is concerned by what sources suggested was an attempt to bully people and companies out of working in the Falklands .
An oil project known as Sea Lion in the North Falkland Basin in the south Atlantic has the potential to triple the Falklands’ GDP but Argentina’s president, Javier Milei , has vowed to block it. Argentina’s strategy includes attempts to criminalise those involved in Sea Lion and deter other investors.
In its letter, the UK government has urged Interpol to be cautious in its handling of Argentinian requests for detentions, it is understood.
Andrea Clausen, the chief executive of the Falklands government, confirmed that the use of Interpol by Argentina was a threat but added: “One would hope that Interpol wouldn’t necessarily take action.”
She said: “Certainly those of us who have an interest have had a look at certain sections of Interpol’s constitution to see what we think it could mean.”
The chief executive of the Falkland Islands, Dr Andrea Clausen, in the room where Argentinian forces surrendered. Photograph: Sean Smith/The Guardian It is understood that a response from Interpol to the UK government’s correspondence stated that it would respect article 3 of its constitution, which forbids it from undertaking any intervention or activities of a political character.
Interpol screens red notices, which are requests to locate and provisionally arrest a person pending extradition. If circulated to the enforcement agencies, individual member countries then decide whether to act on the requests. Nearly 20,000 were issued last year.
The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has told MPs that the UK will protect businesses working in the Falklands from pressure from Argentina through measures under protection of trading interests (PTI) legislation.
The legislation allows the UK to issue orders and directions forbidding British individuals and companies from complying with specific foreign laws or trade controls. It also opens up the possibility that those affected by Argentinian legal pressure could claim damages in UK courts.
Miliband said: “The UK’s support for the Falkland Islands is steadfast. Argentina’s attempts to intimidate businesses and individuals engaged in legitimate commercial activity are unacceptable. Companies should be free to make lawful commercial decisions without the threat of political coercion.
“We will always stand up for the Falkland Islanders, their right to determine their own future, and their right to pursue legitimate economic development.”
The intensity of Argentinian pressure relating to the Falklands is at a level that UK officials say has not been seen since the war 44 years ago that followed the invasion ordered by the then Argentinian dictator, Gen Leopoldo Galtieri.
The 74-day conflict ended with the surrender of the Argentinian forces and cost the lives of 649 of its military personnel, 255 British military personnel and three Falkland Islanders.
Argentina continues to claim sovereignty over the 700 islands that make up the Falklands and has dismissed a 2013 referendum in which 99.8% of the islands’ 3,600 residents voted to remain a British territory, with only three votes against .
Despite Interpol’s reassurance about its screening of red notice requests, concerns remain that Argentina could convince the organisation’s member states that its requests are not political but rooted in domestic legislation.
Milei has initiated criminal proceedings against the Israeli company Navitas and its British partner, Rockhopper Exploration, which are the core companies in the offshore Sea Lion project.
Containers for housing oil workers on the Falkland Islands. Photograph: Sean Smith/The Guardian A draft national sovereignty bill introduced to Argentina’s congress would further expand the scope of sanctions to affiliates of those companies, financial intermediaries, shareholders and suppliers.
The bill additionally contains clauses that could target those involved in the fishing industry in the Falklands, which makes up a large part of the islands’ economy. The archipelago is 300 miles (500km) east of the southern Patagonian coast of Argentina.
Workers in the oil and fisheries sectors on the Falklands – known in Argentina as Las Malvinas – are understood to be concerned that they could be targeted should they travel, particularly to South America, where there is support for Buenos Aires’s sovereignty claim.
In a tandem move to kill off Sea Lion, Argentina is expected within 24 hours to escalate further its dispute with the UK by requesting arbitration under annex VII of the UN convention on the law of the sea (Unclos) over the oil project.
On 28 September, Milei gave the UK a two-week deadline to stop the project or face such legal action. The deadline passed on Monday and Argentinian newspapers said an application for arbitration would follow.
Under it, Buenos Aires will claim the UK is in breach of a UN resolution inviting the parties to negotiate over the sovereignty dispute and refrain from “unilateral modifications” to the situation. It will be seeking a binding ruling that the UK must stop the drilling. However, UK government sources are confident that Unclos will not wade into a sovereignty dispute.
At a public meeting on Monday evening, one of the Falkland Islands’ assembly members, Dean Dent, told constituents that the UK government was working hard on a tough response to the Argentinian Unclos threat.
“The UK government has assembled quite an in-depth team of legal advisers, KCs – that is the first step,” he said. “There have been four recent similar cases where a case of sovereignty has been taken to Unclos and all four were disregarded by the tribunal as all four cases were a sovereignty issue, not a maritime issue.”
The UK government is expected to be increasingly muscular in its approach to Argentina in the coming days. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, told parliament on Monday that he had raised the issue and “the clear and declared will of the islanders to remain British” with the US president, Donald Trump.

Locking the UK out of the EU’s flagship industrial “Made in Europe” legislation would amount to a “deliberate choice” by EU leaders to “hurt” the car industry across the bloc, the head of Mercedes-Benz has said.
A general view of a production line of German car manufacturer Mercedes-Benz at a factory, in Rastatt, Germany. Photograph: Christoph Steitz/Reuters Speaking in his capacity as president of the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA), Ola Källenius said such a move would “weaken the industry on both sides”.
He was speaking just weeks before political leaders hope to reach agreement on the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA) , potentially keeping the UK car industry out of key contracts in the EU.
The act, known as the Made in Europe law, aims to protect local industry by countering competition from outside the EU.
It is mainly aimed at China , which is now enjoying a £1bn a day trade surplus with the EU, but could cause problems for the EU’s close allies including the UK, Norway, Turkey and Switzerland.
“It does not make any sense … We would hurt our industry in the UK and the EU. That would be a deliberate choice to worsen the competitiveness of your own [EU] industry,” Källenius said at an annual briefing in Brussels on the state of the car industry.
“We are talking about how we industrialise more in Europe, how we build local supply chains, that is what the IAA is all about,” he added.
Andy Burnham has been lobbying hard to get the UK included in the Made in Europe legislation but is hitting resistance, particularly from France.

Meanwhile, France’s foreign minister has accused Elon Musk of using his social media platform to orchestrate “massive online harassment campaigns” against European leaders as he took aim at foreign efforts to destabilise the country before next year’s presidential election.
Elon Musk reacts as president-elect Donald Trump speaks at a rally ahead of the presidential inauguration in January last year. Photograph: Alex Brandon/AP Speaking at an Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development conference on Tuesday, Jean-Noël Barrot pointed to the role that social media had come to play in the global battle over democracy.
“ The forces seeking to undermine democracy now dominate the information landscape , where they employ tactics designed to polarise public debate,” he said .
The result was that “political movements with authoritarian aims”, which “play right into the hands of democracy’s declared enemies”, had been gaining ground in Europe and North America, he said.
France's foreign minister Jean-Noël Barrot during a session of questions to the government at the French National Assembly in Paris earlier today. Photograph: Thomas Samson/AFP/Getty Images “They exacerbate the polarisation of our societies,” he added. “Their ultimate goal is clear: to seize power and then create the conditions to never relinquish it.”
Barrot cited the 2027 presidential election in France, where the far-right leader Marine Le Pen is the frontrunner in the polls .
“The enemies of democracy are doing everything they can to destabilise us,” he said. “They exploit our divisions and use immigration, secularism and the Israeli-Palestinian conflict to stoke hatred and tensions.”

Andy Burnham will host Volodymyr Zelenskyy at Downing Street on Wednesday as the UK seeks to further underline its support for the Ukrainian president, in contrast to his difficulties with Donald Trump.
Zelenskyy and Burnham during their meeting in late August Photograph: Ukrainian Presidency/SIPA/Shutterstock The UK prime minister said his message to Zelenskyy and his country would be: “We are with you for as long as it takes.”
To coincide with the visit, the UK has said it will move more rapidly in providing Ukraine with British-made lightweight multi-role missiles (LMMs) to help protect it from attacks by a new generation of Russian jet-powered drones.
In parallel, Burnham and his ministers will push for a full international maritime services ban on exports of Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG).
The pair have already met twice since Burnham took office in July, when Zelenskyy visited a naval base in Portsmouth in the same month and when Burnham travelled to Kyiv in August.
Zelenskyy’s latest visit comes as Ukraine faces increased Russian missile and drone attacks, and after Donald Trump made a deal to buy Russian diesel, called for Ukraine to have a new leader , and announced a supposed ceasefire connected to energy infrastructure that the Ukrainian president said “was news to him”.
Burnham to host Zelenskyy at No 10 in show of ‘rock-solid’ support
UK prime minister Andy Burnham said he will seek to “repair bridges” between US president Donald Trump and Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy amid strained ties between the pair , AFP reported.
Britain’s prime minister Andy Burnham speaking during the ‘Prime Minister’s Questions’ (PMQs) in parliament in central London. Photograph: PRU/AFP/Getty Images Burnham made the comments before he was due to welcome Zelensky to his official Downing Street residence, in a show of support for Ukraine’s president after new criticism by Trump.
“What I have to do in my role is try and repair bridges so that the support comes back ,” Burnham told the British parliament.
“Therefore I should, at this moment in time, be careful in terms of laying the ground to bring people back together. That is the role I intend to play.”
The pair is expected to meet this afternoon, and the Ukrainian president is also expected to meet King Charles III.
Interestingly, Zelenskyy departed for London from the Polish city in Rzeszów reverting to flying from Poland after months of flying from Moldova’s Chișinău during a period of strained relations with Poland over history.

In pretty pointed remarks against the surging far-right Alternative fur Deutschland, Merz also recalls the opening line from the 1950 Schuman declaration, which said:
“World peace cannot be safeguarded without the making of creative efforts proportionate to the dangers which threaten it.”
German chancellor Friedrich Merz speaks during a session of the German parliament, the Bundestag, to deliver a government statement in Berlin, Germany. Photograph: Filip Singer/EPA Adapting it to today’s Germany and Europe , Merz urges parties to recommit to that “creative effort” and not “a scornful desire for disintegration, a delight in division, or exclusion or fear of others.”
“ We must summon that effort and we will - not least in the face of the extremism that has always been a part of our society and is now surging with full force into this parliament, into state parliaments, and into the everyday life of our country.”
He acknowledges that “this extremism … has roots in legitimate dissatisfaction and legitimate feelings of injustices,” but insists it would not resolve any of the people’s problems.
Over in Berlin, Germany’s embattled chancellor Friedrich Merz is addressing the Bundestag, talking about his government’s plan of reforms, his plans for this week’s EU summit in Brussels and Ukraine .
German chancellor Friedrich Merz delivers a speech during a plenum session of the lower house of parliament, the Bundestag in Berlin, Germany. Photograph: Fabrizio Bensch/Reuters He warns lawmakers that Germany faces “a time of upheaval, with crises and wars, some of which lie beyond our control.”
Merz repeats his key lines on the much-needed investment in Germany’s defence capabilities, and doubles down on his support for Ukraine.
He dismisses any suggestion that Germany’s support for Ukraine comes at an expense of social and welfare spending.
“This is simply not a case. Not a single euro flowing to Ukraine is being diverted from social or educational spending in our own country. Not a single euro, ” he said.
Merz warns that “the danger is very real and concrete,” as Russia continues to show “willigness to escalate: against Ukraine, against our eastern European neighbours, and indeed against our own country.”
“Against this backdrop … it is incomprehensible to me how those on the far left and far right continue to play down the situation, ” he said.
He says some comments were almost “deliberately driving the division … and disinformation” to “derivse partisan, political advantages from it.”
Chancellor Friedrich Merz delivering a government statement at the Bundestag in Berlin. Photograph: dts News Agency Germany/Shutterstock Turning to this week’s EU summit, Merz says the discussions will focus on the next EU budget with “negotiations now entering a decisive phase.”
He stresses Germany’s priorities of security and competitiveness , with a call to “further cut back EU bureaucracy and accelerate approval processes to boost and enable investment across Europe ,” particularly in decarbonisation, AI and defence.
He also talks about the importance of a new legal regime for pan-European startups , advancing the EU’s capital markets union, and on developing new trade relationships with global partners while reducing “one-sided dependencies” with existing partners.
“ We will no longer stand idly by while other states harm our economy through heavy subsidies, artificially devalued currencies, overcapacity, and aggressive pricing. We will not stand idly by any longer.”
His comments come ahead of his planned trips to Japan, South Korea and Singapore.
He says the European Council will discuss creating “a new trade defence instrument” to respond “swiftly and forcefully to targeted attacks on our industries and supply chains.”
“These decisions would, among other things, provide the European Commission with a tool to react rapidly without needing to consult the European Council first. The European Council, for its part, would then have the power to reverse such a move by a qualified majority. This makes us faster and more effective, and gives the Commission a powerful tool.”
Over in Germany, we have an update on the Nord Stream trial which began in Hamburg earlier today ( 10:43 ).
Serhii Kuznietsov, centre, a former Ukrainian army officer, attends a trial at the Hanseatic Higher Regional Court in Hamburg, Germany. Photograph: Hannibal Hanschke/EPA Defence lawyers for a former Ukrainian army officer charged with damaging the Nord Stream gas pipelines in blasts four years ago have called for the dismissal of charges in the first day of his trial.
Moving to have the case dismissed, Serhii Kuznetsov’s lawyer Nicola Canestrini argued that the pipeline — which provided half of Germany’s imports of natural gas before Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine — was a “Russian weapon” and therefore potentially a legitimate target, Reuters reported.
“Is it unlawful to destroy an aggressor’s infrastructure without harming any human beings?”
Kuznietsov’s lawyers also argued that he was still an active duty solider an as such was obligated by Ukrainian law not to speak about anything during his service for reasons of secrecy linked to national security, AP reported.
Protesters gathered outside the Hamburg court in support of the defendant, with a sign that read: “What are war crimes?”
Ukraine supporters gather at the entrance to the Hanseatic Higher Regional Court in Hamburg, Germany. Photograph: Markus Scholz/DPA/AP “Russia ‌is the only war criminal that belongs in the dock,” said one of the dozens of protesters.
In the Bulgarian parliament, prime minister Rumen Radev has said that Russia was most likely behind drone attacks in the Black Sea that sank two ships, but that “we cannot prove it”.
AP quotes Radev saying “There is no logic in Ukraine attacking its own ships and crews, given that the outcome of all these attacks favours Russia, and indeed, the logic points in that direction. The problem is that we cannot prove it.”
The Russian ambassador to Bulgaria was summoned yesterday over the issue, and Bulgarian president Iliana Yotova has called for an immediate halt to hostilities in the Black Sea and a moratorium on drone attacks against commercial and civilian infrastructure.
Bulgaria is investigating a report that several antennas used for communication with the Starlink satellite network were deliberately set on fire, prime minister Rumen Radev has said.
“The investigation is extremely intensive. We are working with partner services to successfully carry out this operation,” AFP reports Radev said in parliament, without confirming or denying the claim.
A Bulgarian opposition MP has claimed 11 telecommunications antennas linked to the Starlink network were set on fire over the weekend “at a secret facility near Sofia”.
A spokesperson for the Sofia prosecutor’s office confirmed to AFP that an investigation was under way but said no one has been charged.
A fire broke out at a Starlink satellite communications station in central Poland in September, with the country’s digital affairs minister calling the blaze an act of “sabotage” and prime minister Donald Tusk describing it as an “act of hybrid warfare”.
A Ukrainian serviceman prepares a Starlink satellite internet system earlier this year. Photograph: Reuters Germany’s foreign minister, Johann Wadephul , has said his country has not observed a substantial reduction in US support for Ukraine , and does not expect to. The statement comes amid the US and Russia having secured a diesel supply deal, and reports that Elon Musk’s Starlink service has been reduced for Ukrainian forces.
Moscow has said that the US-Russia deal over diesel “will open other ⁠opportunities as ​well”.
Reuters reports Kremlin ⁠envoy Kirill ​Dmitriev said Moscow would overcome any sanctions-related difficulties to ensure the ‌diesel supplies were delivered, and that the deal could pave the ⁠way ​for further economic ⁠cooperation between the two nations.
Reuters, citing local media, reports that Bulgaria expects to join a Nato anti-drone initiative by the end of October . The news comes a day after a drone attack sank a cargo vessel off the country’s Black Sea ⁠coast for the second ⁠time in ​a week.
Defence minister Dimitar ⁠Stoyanov said “Bulgaria will be part of this ⁠project as soon as possible. Expectations are that by 30 October, we will already ​be part of the project.”
And Reuters is reporting that shares in European satellite operator Eutelsat ⁠rose sharply on Wednesday after Ukraine said SpaceX’s Starlink ⁠had introduced ⁠restrictions ​on its military-grade service, fuelling investor bets that European providers ⁠could benefit from growing strains between Washington and Kyiv.
Eutelsat ⁠shares were up 11.6% by ​late morning, ‌while Luxembourg-based rival ‌SES, which also provides satellite connectivity ‌services, gained 2.7%.
The European Commission declined to comment on reported disruption to Starlink’s services in Ukraine , but said there are “no indication that [US] intelligence sharing has stopped.”
Repeatedly asked about the issue, the commission spokespeople said they were “aware of the report” on Starlink, but declined to comment “until we have more information.”
“[It is] important also to say that we have no indications that, intelligence sharing has stopped,” the chief spokesperson, Paula Pinho, said.
The European Commission has warned that the EU is “headed for a very, very difficult winter” with high energy prices expected to cause an affordability crisis and “a very volatile” in the energy markets.
A digital billboard displays fuel prices at a petrol station in Berlin, Germany. Photograph: John MacDougall/AFP/Getty Images The warning was delivered by the EU’s energy spokesperson Anna-Kaisa Itkonen when answering questions about proposed changes adding flexibility to rules on methane imports to help save costs.
She stressed the EU was “not facing a security supply issue for the time being,” but it faced a “very unpredictable” situation in the coming months.
“We do not have visibility, for example, what and when something will happen in the Strait of Hormuz, where 20% of gas and oil is being blocked since many, many months,” she said.
The commission’s chief spokesperson, Paula Pinho, added that the changes are needed as “we could not anticipate that we would have a crisis in the Strait of Hormuz,” which continues to affect prices and supply of energy.
This summer in Germany, Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) booked a historic state election victory in Saxony-Anhalt. Meanwhile, support for far-right parties has been growing across Europe.
‘It starts here’ banner at the AfD election party for the 2026 Saxony-Anhalt state election in Germany. Photograph: dts News Agency Germany/Shutterstock There are now radical right, populist parties in coalition governments in Croatia, Czechia, Italy and Finland, and leading in the polls in Austria, Belgium, France and Germany.
The coming months will see further crucial elections, beginning in Spain in November and continuing in France, Estonia, Finland, Greece, Slovakia, Poland and Italy next year. How might these elections shape the political future of the continent?
Jon Henley and Ashifa Kassam, our European correspondents, will be answering your questions live on Reddit r/geopolitics from 4pm CEST.

France’s foreign minister has accused Elon Musk of using his social media platform to orchestrate “massive online harassment campaigns” against European leaders as he took aim at foreign efforts to destabilise the country before next year’s presidential election.
Speaking at an Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development conference on Tuesday, Jean-Noël Barrot pointed to the role that social media had come to play in the global battle over democracy. “The forces seeking to undermine democracy now dominate the information landscape, where they employ tactics designed to polarise public debate,” he said .
The result was that “political movements with authoritarian aims”, which “play right into the hands of democracy’s declared enemies”, had been gaining ground in Europe and North America, he said.
“They exacerbate the polarisation of our societies,” he added. “Their ultimate goal is clear: to seize power and then create the conditions to never relinquish it.”
Jean-Noël Barrot said the goal of the campaigns was clear: ‘to seize power and then create the conditions to never relinquish it’. Photograph: Olivier Hoslet/EPA Barrot cited the 2027 presidential election in France, where the far-right leader Marine Le Pen is the frontrunner in the polls . “The enemies of democracy are doing everything they can to destabilise us,” he said. “They exploit our divisions and use immigration, secularism and the Israeli-Palestinian conflict to stoke hatred and tensions.”
He listed several other examples, from an unnamed Israeli company accused of creating fake French social media accounts to influence perceptions of the Israel-Gaza war, to accusations that Azerbaijan stirred up tensions amid deadly riots in the French Pacific territory New Caledonia.
Barrot also singled out Musk, the world’s richest man and owner of the social media platform X . “There are massive online harassment campaigns launched by Elon Musk against European leaders in order to influence debates by exploiting the virality of his social media platform.”
Barrot also cited the protests that have rocked France in recent weeks , as schoolchildren, students and trade unionists blockaded schools and marched through cities . The events, said Barrot, had been exploited by “hostile narratives” from Russia, China and Iran, as well as those associated with the Maga movement in the US.
Barrot cited the recent schools protests as another event that had been exploited by ‘hostile narratives’ coming from Russia, China, Iran and those associated with the Maga movement in the US. Photograph: Firas Abdullah/EPA Last week Musk and the US president, Donald Trump, weighed in on the protests in France , seeking to recast them through a lens of mass migration and brushing aside protesters’ demands for better school conditions.
How the ‘poisonous tide’ of disinformation spreads division and despair
Barrot said his government was working to respond to a reality in which paid or commissioned influencers sought to explore the viral reach of digital platforms. “The Kremlin’s goal is explicitly stated: to put an end to our liberal democracies in favour of a new authoritarianism. Other actors are converging on this goal, seeking to dictate to Europe which democracies are ‘good’ and which are ‘bad’ based on whether they align with their own interests,” he said.
The French minister’s remarks come days after the British prime minister, Andy Burnham, said it was “clear” that Russia had interfered in the Brexit referendum.
Barrot said his government would work to counter these efforts by foreign entities. “We are uncompromising, because it is clear to us that they undermine the nation’s fundamental interests,” he said. “We do not tolerate any foreign interference, from wherever it may come. It is a matter of sovereignty.”
